paras: The lynching at Gallup, New Mexico, was the killing of an unnamed man by a mob at Gallup in early 1888, after he was accused of murdering one or both of his gambling companions. It is known from a single second-hand item, credited to the Optic and reprinted in the Arizona Silver Belt on February 25, 1888, which drew notice for the mob's use of a passenger coach's bell cord in place of a rope.

According to the account, three men were gambling at Gallup when the loser "became enraged and murdered one or both of his companions." An "excited mob" then gathered and "at once lynched the murderer." Lacking a rope, the mob cut the bell cord out of a coach of a passenger train that was stopped at Gallup at the time. The item gives no names, no date and no race for any of the men involved.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage.

The story reached print through Mrs. Lieutenant Glassford, a passenger in the coach from which the cord was taken, who "brings word of a deed of violence" to the Optic. The Arizona Silver Belt reprinted the item on its first page, crediting the Optic, and the writer hedged its accuracy with the words "If we caught the story correctly." The item called the victim "the murderer" and offered no comment on the mob's action.
No other newspaper report of the episode appears in the coverage.

The only report is A1, a short reprint from the Optic of a passenger's account; no second report was found.

accounts.label: Passenger's account via the Optic
accounts.gist: Three men were gambling; the loser killed one or both companions, and an excited mob at once lynched him with the coach bell cord. The writer hedges on whether he caught the story correctly.

framing.detail: A short news item calling it 'a deed of violence' and the victim 'the murderer', without comment on the mob, reprinted from the Optic.

Two or three: the lynched man plus 'one or both' companions.
An 'excited mob', unnamed and of unstated size.
